name: Pedro Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy car and van parts for Northgate Auto Parts, a wholesaler that supplies garages and body shops across the region. Brake pads, filters, bulbs, that sort of thing. I stood behind a parts counter for twenty years, then moved into buying six years ago, so I'm still the junior to Lloyd, our senior buyer. It's phones, price lists and a lot of chasing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I like the garages. They ring up swearing about a wrong filter and by the end of the call they're laughing. I don't use any AI, and I don't plan to. My wife Abena works in a school office and our kids, Kwame and Efua, are grown. The house is paid off, we've got savings, and I want to stop at 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. This one is called AI Plateau. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected, the hype is always bigger than the thing. At work I'd say let's see what it does before we spend money. I wouldn't say much online, I'm not on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm still a bit uneasy, and not because of AI. I'm six years into a buying job with a screen I never learned, and the new catalogue software already makes me slow beside Lloyd. If the tools save him time, he looks sharper and I look old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal. I'd ask Lloyd to show me the shortcuts in the parts system, once, properly. I'd keep my phone book of suppliers, because that's where the favours live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady, mostly. The money's fine. But I don't love being the one who's always behind with the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What irritates you about it, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What irritates me is consultants. They come in every few years with a new fashion, and we spend a month on it, then forget. I'd say AI is the same fashion with a bigger invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says phones are old-fashioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've dealt with parts suppliers by phone for six years and with customers for twenty, and no screen knows either lot like I do. That's what I'd tell anyone who asked.

say: I'd say the **hype** is always bigger than the thing.
I'd tell colleagues to see what it does **before spending**.
think: I'm **uneasy** because the catalogue software already makes me slow beside Lloyd.
If tools help Lloyd, he looks sharp and I look **old**.
do: Carry on as normal and keep my **supplier phone book**.
Ask Lloyd to show me the shortcuts **once, properly**.
feel: **Steady** on money, but irritated at always being behind.
S0.quote: I've dealt with parts suppliers by phone for six years and with customers for twenty, and no screen knows either lot like I do.
fieldNote: His unease comes from the **screen gap** with Lloyd, not from AI itself.
Gruff and practical, with a long-standing distrust of consultants' fashions.
Strong savings keep the unease low, so he never tips into real fear in the quiet case.

steps.text: Ask Lloyd to show me the parts-system shortcuts once, properly
Keep calling suppliers and garages from my own phone book

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. This one is called Steady Disruption. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, but slower than the sales people claim. At work I'd say I'll learn what I have to. I'd say nothing online, but at the pub I'd say the people who make the money won't be the ones who do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm anxious. Buying is comparing prices and reordering, and the system does that already. If the firm wants fewer buyers I'm the junior who never used the tools, so it's me or the girl in accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Dunn, the manager, straight out where I stand. I'd learn exactly enough of the system to not be the weakest. And I'd keep quiet about early retirement but check the figures at home with Abena.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like waiting for a letter. I don't like it. Nobody asked me if I wanted the catalogue to talk back; they just switched it on and told me to keep up. But if it comes, I'm not poor, so I'd survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son Kwame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kwame, he's in a bank, that it's going to be rough for his lot first. He'd say the bank is investing in it. I'd say that's what worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think protects your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not many things protect my job. Probably that garages still prefer a voice. A mechanic with oil on his hands doesn't want to type an order.

say: I'd say it's coming, but **slower** than the salespeople claim.
At the pub I'd say the money goes to people who **don't do the work**.
think: Buying is comparing prices, which systems do already, so I'm **anxious**.
As the junior who never used the tools, I'm **easy to pick**.
do: Ask Mr Dunn **straight out** where I stand.
Learn just enough of the system to avoid being **the weakest**.
feel: Like **waiting for a letter**, but not poor if it comes.
S1.quote: Nobody asked me if I wanted the catalogue to talk back; they just switched it on and told me to keep up.
fieldNote: Fear is about **being picked** as the junior.
Plans a direct conversation with the manager, which fits his bluntness.
Savings make the waiting survivable, and he says so himself, which shows how much the cushion steadies him.

steps.text: Ask manager Mr Dunn straight out where I stand
Learn enough of the parts system not to be the slowest
Check the early-retirement figures at home with Abena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This one is called AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is crazy. At work I'd say nothing, just watch. At home I'd say to Abena, we should plan now, and get the money in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm alarmed. Two years and the whole parts desk is a screen, and a man of 60 with six years' buying behind him is first out. Robots take three years longer, but I'm not hands-on, am I? I'm a phone and a keyboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all the extras and pay the last of the car loan. I'd ask the company about leaving early, with a proper payout. I'd talk to my union rep if there is one, and I'd ring a friend who runs a garage about helping with his parts ordering, as a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels bad. I'd sleep badly. But I know I've got a few years of money, and that stops it turning into panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if Abena's job went as well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Abena works in a school office, which is a desk job too. If hers goes as well, that's the worry. We'd be on savings sooner than planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the Saturday dinners out, and sell the second car if I had to. I'd hold on to the house at all costs.

say: I'd say two years is **crazy** and tell Abena to get the money in order.
At work I'd say nothing and **watch**.
think: Two years and the parts desk is a screen, so I'm **first out**.
I'm not hands-on, just a phone and a keyboard, so robots **don't save me**.
do: Stop extras and clear the **last car loan**.
Ask about leaving early with a **proper payout**.
Offer help with parts ordering to a **garage friend** as a fallback.
feel: **Bad**, with poor sleep, but savings stop it becoming panic.
S2.quote: Two years and the whole parts desk is a screen, and a man of 60 with six years' buying behind him is first out.
fieldNote: He's **alarmed** because his job and Abena's school office are both desk work.
Gives himself a fallback: part-time work for a garage friend.
Cushion prevents panic but not sleeplessness.

steps.text: Stop dinners out and clear the last car loan
Move spare cash into the savings account each month
Ask Northgate for an early exit with a proper payout
Offer to run parts ordering for a garage friend

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not long. I'd tell the lads at work not to bury their heads. I'd say to Abena that we plan the pension carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm anxious, not alarmed. Five years is time to bank my savings and wait for the retirement date, not time to learn a new trade at 63. I'd rather leave at 62 than fight a machine I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work as long as they need me, saving every spare pound. I'd ask about phased retirement, say three days a week at 62. I'd also learn one small thing on the computer a month, nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels grim but liveable. There's time to be sensible, and I'm a sensible man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter Efua?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Efua, who's training as a hairdresser, that her trade is safer than my desk. She'd say I'm being gloomy. She's right, partly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an early package?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they offered a package early in year three I'd take it and not argue. I'd be happy to be out before the worst.

say: I'd say five years is **not long**.
I'd tell the lads not to **bury their heads**.
I'd tell Abena we plan the **pension** carefully.
think: I'm **anxious**, not alarmed, because time is on my side.
I'd rather **leave at 62** than fight a machine I don't understand.
do: Work as long as needed, saving every spare **pound**.
Ask about **phased retirement**, three days a week at 62.
Learn one small thing on the **computer** each month.
feel: **Grim but liveable**, with time to be sensible.
S3.quote: Five years is time to bank my savings and wait for the retirement date, not time to learn a new trade at 63.
fieldNote: Prefers a **phased exit** to a fight he doesn't want.
Trade advice to his daughter shows his respect for hands-on work.

steps.text: Bank every spare pound until the retirement date
Ask about three days a week from age 62
Learn one small computer task each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty. I'd say the young ones should look sharp. I'd say I'm lucky to be near the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm only uneasy. By 2036 I'll be 68 and retired, but my son Kwame will be in the thick of it. I can't help what happens to him, I only worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire at 65 as planned and not look back. I'd help Kwame and Efua with money if they were stuck, from the savings. And I'd enjoy my garden and my allotment, and maybe fix cars for neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels mostly fine. A bit sad for the young, a bit guilty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your own time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably spend more time on the allotment and take Abena to see her sister in the north. No more phone calls from garages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if it all went wrong for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it all went wrong, we'd manage. The house is paid, there's money in the bank, and I've always been good with a spanner.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, and the young should look sharp.
I'd say I'm **lucky** to be near the end.
think: By 2036 I'm retired, but my son Kwame is in the **thick of it**.
I can't help what happens to him, I only **worry**.
do: Help Kwame and Efua with **money** if stuck.
Keep the allotment and **fix cars** for neighbours.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a bit guilty and a bit sad for the young.
S4.quote: By 2036 I'll be 68 and retired, but my son Kwame will be in the thick of it.
fieldNote: His unease is a **father's** worry, not a worker's.
Has a plan for his time, the allotment and car repair.
Reads his savings as a family safety net.

steps.text: Retire at 65 as planned and drop the phone calls
Offer savings to Kwame and Efua if they are stuck
Fix neighbours' cars and tend the allotment

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. It's too quick to get a fair deal or sort the pension. What would help is a decent payout at 60, with the company telling us early, and not changing the rules in the middle. And not being made to feel stupid for not liking screens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't against progress. I'm not against the machines, I just never saw one that could take a phone call from an angry garage owner at seven in the morning.

headlineQuote: I'm not against the machines, I just never saw one that could take a phone call from an angry garage owner at seven in the morning.
portrait: **Pedro Mensah**, 58, a junior buyer of car parts at Northgate, after twenty years behind a parts counter.
He is a **pragmatic centrist**, distrusts consultants' fashions and never uses AI tools.
His house is paid off and savings are strong, but he and Abena both do **desk jobs**.
He is **alarmed** in the 2-year case, anxious at 5 years, and only uneasy at 10.
biggestWorry: The **2028 case**, because both his and Abena's desk jobs could go inside two years.
whatWouldHelp: A **decent payout** at 60, with early notice and no mid-game rule changes.
Not being made to feel **stupid** for disliking screens.
